method: Complete candidate survey followed by individual editorial choices and written reasons, applied to the existing complete guide to keep it within 300 quotations. All verified authorized selections included. Priority given to foundational teachings, substantive explanations, necessary qualifications, distinctive applications, narrative examples and thematic breadth across trustworthiness with other people’s funds, consultation and accurate accounts, work and enterprise as service, partnership and proportion, livelihood, receipts and financial records, debt and mercy, inheritance and reconciliation, wills and gifts, assistance to particular lives, building funds, property and title, trading under pressure, travel, daily supplies, laws in their distinct settings, and spiritual commerce. Neither citation count nor source order used as a ranking rule. The existing reading arc is retained.

selected.text: the doors of blessing will open even in business and commerce
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s brief promise that the doors of blessing will open even in business and commerce; links spiritual blessing with ordinary trade.

selected.text: this new company … its resources … gates of ease and expansion
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer for a new company’s resources and gates of ease and expansion; the guide’s closing prayer.

selected.text: With regard to his life insurance, act in accordance with his will.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a life insurance policy be handled according to the deceased’s will; a modern instrument governed by the will.

selected.text: He has copies on hand and is in debt and deserves consideration and assistance
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá commends a believer in debt as deserving consideration and assistance; mercy toward a debtor.

selected.text: The intent of these words is that there should be no negligence in paying debts.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter states plainly that there should be no negligence in paying debts; a concise rule.

selected.text: Prepare a place for her and the children so they may rest there in comfort and tranquility.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a place be prepared for a mother and children to rest in comfort; shelter as an act of care.

selected.text: make some arrangement for his livelihood so that the small amount he has does not run out
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a livelihood be arranged for a man so that his small capital does not run out; protecting modest means.

selected.text: Keep with you the extra receipts that were sent to you by Jinab-i-Afnan, and deliver the enclosed letters
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that extra receipts be kept and enclosed letters delivered; the routine of financial correspondence.

selected.text: that what is commonly recited at the pilgrims' return be replaced with the verses of truth. I am but a man among merchants who consider the profit of wealth
selected.reason: The Báb, in a letter to His uncle, calls Himself a man among merchants; the Báb’s own mercantile setting.

selected.text: Keep this Baha'i children's company perpetual and continuous, and make it blessed and profitable
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays that a Bahá’í children’s company be perpetual, blessed and profitable; a striking example of enterprise among children.

selected.text: please endeavor to provide assistance to other peoples, especially if the government makes a request
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges assistance to other peoples, especially at the government’s request; generosity beyond one’s own community.

selected.text: Complete the accounts with Bombay likewise … And pay the price for it so the account may be settled
selected.reason: The Báb asks that accounts with Bombay be completed and a price paid so the account may be settled; further evidence of the Báb’s practice in commerce.

selected.text: The next morning the owner of the plot himself came to Me, apologized and begged Me to purchase his property.
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: you must serve the honored bank president with the utmost sincerity, diligence, zeal, goodwill and truthfulness
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks an employee to serve the bank president with sincerity, diligence, goodwill and truthfulness; the virtues expected of a worker.

selected.text: Regarding your question about consultation between father and son and son with father in business and commerce
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers a question on consultation between father and son in business and commerce; introduces the guide’s theme of shared judgment in enterprise.

selected.text: Whoever pays the Huquq must obtain a receipt from whomever they send it through, so that the work may be orderly.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that whoever pays the Huqúq obtain a receipt so that the work may be orderly; the guide’s basic rule of receipts.

selected.text: secretly deliver one hundred tumans each year through a confidential note … send fifty tumans for Mulla Ahmad-'Ali
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs a secret yearly gift through a confidential note; discretion in charity.

selected.text: Should any sum be required for a certain matter, you must certainly arrange and deliver it, even if it be as a loan
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a needed sum be delivered even as a loan; ensuring help arrives.

selected.text: The Covenant Partnership is a manifestation of the favors of the All-Merciful and the recipient of endless bounties.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the Covenant Partnership a manifestation of the favors of the All-Merciful; praise of a named cooperative enterprise.

selected.text: Henceforth if they send telegrams, they should pay double the fee so it will definitely arrive and request a reply.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises paying a double fee on telegrams to ensure arrival and a reply; a small practical detail of reliable communication.

selected.text: Regarding the expenses that some had written about, I swear by God that in these days not even a small amount exists
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá swears that no funds exist for expenses requested; honesty about scarcity.

selected.text: As for the disorder in thy material affairs, it is hoped that these too shall be set right through divine aid and favor
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes disorder in material affairs will be set right through divine aid; hope amid difficulty.

selected.text: Continue to deliver his lifetime allowance to his family and dependents after him so that they may not be left in need.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a lifetime allowance continue to a man’s family after him; enduring provision for dependents.

selected.text: Regarding the properties, let them exercise some patience until the boundary issue between Iran and Turkey is resolved.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counsels patience over properties until a boundary issue is resolved; timing amid uncertainty.

selected.text: If you undertake any worldly endeavors, the purpose is to obtain some blessing that may be spent in praiseworthy causes
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá states that the purpose of worldly endeavor is to obtain blessings that may be spent in praiseworthy causes; names the purpose of enterprise.

selected.text: Jinab-i-Aqa 'Abbasquli endowed three thousand square cubits of land on Mount Carmel as a dedication to the Sacred Shrine
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá records an endowment of land on Mount Carmel to the Shrine; dedication of property.

selected.text: Thus, when they bring two words of consent from him each month, deliver five tumans each month to Aqa Mirza 'Ali-Muhammad.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sets a monthly payment conditioned on proof of the recipient’s consent; assistance with stated conditions.

selected.text: Also record whatever special funds were spent and lost in this transaction, so that it may be known how much remains today
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh asks that funds spent and lost in a transaction be recorded to show what remains; candid accounting of loss.

selected.text: The debt of Alexandria and Haifa hath been discharged, for the sum hath been received, and the receipts that thou hadst previously requested have been sent
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: They brought two thousand two hundred pieces of gold at a time when means were entirely lacking, and it was spent in that place
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá records two thousand two hundred pieces of gold brought when means were entirely lacking and spent where needed; timely support in scarcity.

selected.text: free his house from mortgage and assist his family to the extent possible so that living expenses may reach his wife and children
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a house be freed from mortgage and living expenses reach a wife and children; concrete care for a family.

selected.text: did not seek to gather worldly goods nor acquire the ornaments of this abode of sorrows, but rather sought to dwell near Thee and spread Thy remembrance and praise. They became renowned among the nations for their
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer for souls who did not seek worldly goods but nearness to God; spiritual priorities.

selected.text: Write to Ibn-i-Ismi, upon them both be My glory, that his honor M.S. must deliver the Huququ'llah and not give it to the oppressors.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter directs that Ḥuqúqu’lláh be delivered and not given to oppressors; faithful handling of sacred funds.

selected.text: Your honor should temporarily proceed to Tehran due to the matter of the purchased land, as someone has claimed it was a conditional sale.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sends a believer to Tehran to defend a land purchase claimed as a conditional sale; securing title.

selected.text: Regarding the matter of Jinab-i-Samandar, this servant submits this promised amount with utmost embarrassment and hopes it will be accepted
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá submits a promised amount with embarrassment, hoping it will be accepted; humility in giving.

selected.text: We rented the palace for thirty years until we bought it … So I had to buy land and make a guesthouse for travelers … claimed right of pre-emption
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reported words on renting a palace and buying land for a guesthouse; hospitality through property.

selected.text: However much they wish to give funds, let them take 22 from the Siyyid's portion. In all matters they should watch over the affairs of the household.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter directs funds from a portion and asks that the household’s affairs be watched over; care for a household.

selected.text: The contribution of the honored Afnan and Jinab-i-Aqa Husayn-'Ali and Jinab-i-Haji Ahmad in paying off your debts was a service to the Cause of God.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the contribution of friends toward paying a believer’s debts a service to the Cause; mutual help in debt.

selected.text: Settle these accounts with Aqa Azizu'llah in such a way that it becomes a cause of dignity for the Cause of God among both the friends and strangers.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that accounts be settled so as to bring dignity to the Cause among friends and strangers; the reputational stake of honest settlement.

selected.text: this Pen has become like the treasury of the Ottomans and Persians - from the abundance of allowances and stipends it has beaten the drum of bankruptcy
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likens his pen to a bankrupt treasury from the abundance of allowances; a financial metaphor for correspondence.

selected.text: Now the funds must be accumulated, the land entirely paid for and the necessary preparations for building made and then the accessory matters considered.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that funds be accumulated, land paid for and preparations made before building; the guide’s sequence of raising funds before projects.

selected.text: If letters arrive, send them to San Francisco in California, and whenever your carpets arrive, telegraph me immediately, for I wish to be the first buyer.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks to be telegraphed when carpets arrive so that he may be the first buyer; a warm example of supporting a believer’s trade.

selected.text: Regarding the purchase of property and its cost which thou didst inquire about - We did not wish to mention this matter as it would cause hardship to some.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh declines to mention a property’s cost lest it cause hardship to some; sensitivity in financial requests.

selected.text: You had complained about the stagnation of trade. In this year, calamities and the blow of economic depression and corruption have encompassed all horizons
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes that calamity and economic depression have encompassed all horizons; places personal trade troubles in a wider crisis.

selected.text: You should, by whatever means possible, provide him with the expenses for gilding, binding and other costs, so that he will not need assistance from others.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that publication costs be provided so the author needs no help from others; support for dignified work.

selected.text: The Muttahidih Company must be as precise as the hands of the clock and exert the utmost effort that it may bring joy and gladness to 'Abdu'l-Baha
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the Muttahidih Company to be as precise as the hands of a clock; a memorable image of exactness in business.

selected.text: Regarding the attainment of blessings in commerce, God willing, its brilliant effects will become manifest through humble supplication at the Divine Threshold.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá links blessings in commerce to humble supplication; prayer for useful work.

selected.text: If in that land the means of livelihood become available, it would be most excellent. We beseech God that He may assist thee and cause suitable means to appear.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh prays that suitable means of livelihood may appear for a believer; a prayerful frame for the search for work.

selected.text: Regarding the dispute over inheritance between the Afnan … the house belonged exclusively to him. It was immediately written that it should be divided among the heirs
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a disputed house be divided among the heirs; a ruling for fair inheritance.

selected.text: The friends must act according to the wish and pleasure of the master Jamshid and strive with utmost power in faithfulness, trustworthiness and excellence of service.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends employed by Jamshid to strive in faithfulness, trustworthiness and excellence of service; extends the ethic of the employee.

selected.text: Write to Jinab-i-Aqa Mirza Aqa that he has the choice of being alone or in partnership, and either one is the cause of joy and delight - both are beloved and ordained
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá leaves a believer free to work alone or in partnership, both being beloved; shows that partnership is a matter of choice.

selected.text: This tea was grown and cultivated on your farm … My hope is that through your efforts the cultivation of tea in those regions will expand and spread to other provinces
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá acknowledges tea grown on a believer’s farm and hopes its cultivation will spread to other provinces; a practical example of productive agriculture.

selected.text: Thou shouldst strive to the utmost in the pursuance of business. Thou shouldst do this same also in spreading the Breaths of God. Divide thy time into two parts! Spend one in the business and the other in service to the Kingdom
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counsels striving to the utmost in business and dividing one’s time between business and service to the Kingdom; a memorable balance of livelihood and service.

selected.text: Exert all efforts, together with the friends, that haply through God's grace, some occupation may be arranged for him, be it in other portions of the country or even abroad.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks for every effort, with the friends, to arrange an occupation for a believer even abroad; reinforces shared responsibility for livelihood.

selected.text: an important (or considerable) sum of money must decidedly be prepared in order that work may be begun: that is, at least two or three hundred thousand dollars must be ready.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá states that a considerable sum must be ready before work begins; preparation before construction.

selected.text: O Jinab-i-Amin! Whatever reached you all arrived at the door. If individual receipts are prevented by your occupations, we have sent a general receipt with the names sealed.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sends a general sealed receipt when individual receipts are impractical; a practical solution for acknowledging funds.

selected.text: in all conditions they should fix their gaze upon the highest horizon, and if they are in debt to anyone they must certainly pay it, whether through compensation or otherwise.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter requires that debts be paid in all conditions while fixing one’s gaze on the highest horizon; joins obligation and spiritual focus.

selected.text: the Covenant! Thy letter hath arrived, and likewise the power of attorney which thou hadst sent for Aqa Mirza Muhsin. He hath gone to Jerusalem. God willing, he will return to 'Akka and take measures to purchase the land
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Ask Leticia to come back and offer her a sum that would secure her agreement. Also, the sum needed for Shoghi Effendi and Ruhangiz's school must all be paid by Aqa Mirza Muhsin.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs payments to secure a helper’s return and for Shoghi Effendi’s schooling; practical household provision.

selected.text: Guard thou the shop which hath been opened in Our name for pilgrims, and which is known by My name, if thou be of them that understand. Then strive to manage and improve its affairs.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh charges a believer to guard and improve the shop opened in His name for pilgrims; a distinctive trust in a commercial undertaking.

selected.text: Therefore, the Spiritual Assembly must establish the grave of that luminous temple with the utmost delicacy and refinement, and whatever expenses are incurred, you should present them.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the Spiritual Assembly to establish a grave with refinement and present the costs; institutional care for memorials.

selected.text: One must accept and act accordingly, and must satisfy you so that the matter does not end up in litigation before the judge, for they are in debt and I am obligated to pay these debts.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges satisfying a creditor to avoid litigation, taking the debts upon himself; reconciliation over court action.

selected.text: Concerning the promissory note of Jinab-i-Aqa Mirza Siyavush, since your seal is on the note, Jinab-i-Aqa Siyavush is in the right, even though his father received and spent the amount
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá rules that a promissory note bearing one’s seal binds the signer even if another spent the money; the weight of a signed obligation.

selected.text: What should be done about the 'Liberty Bonds' that were sent as contributions to the Mashrak-ul-Askar fund
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reported words raise the question of Liberty Bonds contributed to the Mashriqu’l-Adhkár fund; practical questions of building funds.

selected.text: his holiness was engaged in the business of indigo. After a short conversation I left him impressed with the loftiness of his ethical standard and the purity of his personal character
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reported words describe meeting one engaged in the indigo business and being impressed by the loftiness of his ethical standard and purity of character; opens the indigo narrative.

selected.text: As commanded, if trade is conducted in a place other than Beirut it would be better and more appropriate. And in whatever place business is conducted, they must act with the utmost wisdom
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh advises that trade be conducted elsewhere than Beirut and always with utmost wisdom; a counsel on location and prudence.

selected.text: God's decree is that if they are found in cities and villages, a crier must make one proclamation and inform the people of that city or village. If the owner is found, they shall return it
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s ruling that found property be proclaimed by a crier and returned to its owner; a provision on lost property.

selected.text: Regarding the location of the office, whatever time the friends of God deem appropriate is acceptable. And concerning partnership with his honor Afnan and his honor Adib, both are suitable
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá leaves the office location to the friends’ judgment and approves either proposed partner; a brief example of practical decisions left to consultation.

selected.text: O thou who art firm in the Covenant! The room that your father endowed must remain, and likewise let the land that your mother endowed remain as a sapling in the garden of the love of God.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a father’s endowed room and a mother’s endowed land remain; fidelity to endowments.

selected.text: the purpose was to arrange for funds to be sent for the repair of the Holy House … fifty French liras, that is one thousand francs, were sent. More than this was not possible at this time
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sends funds for repairing the Holy House as far as possible; care for a sacred place.

selected.text: Some time ago, five hundred tumans was transferred through Jenab-i-Amin in the name of my cousin for building a dam against the river, and no shortcoming will be allowed within possibility.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá records five hundred tumans transferred for building a dam against the river and promises no shortcoming; a practical development undertaking.

selected.text: You had asked whether if someone has land that they cannot develop and its income is less than expenses, is it permissible to sell or mortgage part of this land. It is certainly permissible.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá permits selling or mortgaging part of land that cannot be developed and whose income is less than its expenses; a clear practical ruling on unprofitable property.

selected.text: I hope that the partnership you have formed will become a magnet for divine blessings and that the signs of the bounty of the Divine Unity will become manifest and evident from every direction.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes a newly formed partnership will become a magnet for divine blessings; a concise blessing on cooperative work.

selected.text: Contributions collected for the teaching fund must be used for teaching. Likewise contributions collected for the Mashrekol-Azkar must be used for the Mashrekol-Azkar. These two must not be mixed.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá rules that contributions for the teaching fund and for the Mashriqu’l-Adhkár must each be used for their own purpose and not mixed; a clear principle of fidelity to a donor’s intent.

selected.text: if you could arrange for that great plot of land to have all its transactions completely finalized in the government registry - meaning all eight plots would be registered in the name of the Temple
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that Temple land be fully registered in the government registry; legal security of property.

selected.text: You had written that a group of the friends from that region wish to sever their ties and come to these parts since you are farmers … Therefore it is better that you do not disrupt your work there
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises farmers not to disrupt their work by relocating; stability of livelihood.

selected.text: Regarding their occupation and commerce, they wished that the two brothers would engage in separate work and be independent, and this servant suggested that they consult with you and seek permission.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reports the wish that two brothers work independently and the suggestion that they consult first; a family business decision referred to consultation.

selected.text: a Bazaar was not so commendable and especially if the Believers should sell necessary articles, such as their furniture, etc. The handiwork of children, as an obvious expression of love, might be sold.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reported words caution against a bazaar where believers sell necessities but allow children’s handiwork; fundraising with discernment.

selected.text: Regarding the matter of the hundred tumans which you wrote should not be deducted from the funds of the land of Kha and should be accepted from you - this matter found acceptance in the Most Holy Court.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter records acceptance of a hundred tumans offered personally rather than deducted from a region’s funds; voluntary giving.

selected.text: Regarding the will of the late Haji Abdul-Rahim, carry it out exactly according to his own testament. In these days, as extreme hardship has befallen the Holy Land, if possible send that amount quickly.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a will be carried out exactly according to the testament; fidelity to a testator’s intent.

selected.text: Regarding his house, he owes seventy tumans to one of the friends of God. Since at present it is not possible to pay it from here, whenever the Huquq becomes available there, you should immediately pay it.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a believer’s house debt be paid immediately when funds become available; timely relief of a debt.

selected.text: Regarding the matter of purchasing the specific house, again it hath been revealed from the heaven of God's command: "Soon shall We raise up one who will purchase what thou hast desired, through pure love
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh promises that one will be raised to purchase a desired house through pure love; a spiritual frame for acquisition.

selected.text: Through the endeavors of the friends of the Spiritual Assembly, some occupation must be arranged for him that will bring peace and tranquility to his mind and enable him to continue in his previous services.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the Spiritual Assembly to arrange an occupation that brings a believer peace of mind and lets him continue his services; collective care for livelihood.

selected.text: Concerning what was written about the Huquq, this has been raised to Our hearing. His blessed and exalted Word states: Whatever Huquq was owed by the spiritual elderly servant and you, We have pardoned it all.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh pardons all the Ḥuqúq owed by two believers; mercy within law.

selected.text: Concerning what thou didst write about the Zakat, the Zakat on garden produce is after the deduction of expenses, that is, the garden expenses must be paid, and whatever remains thereafter is subject to Zakat.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that zakát on garden produce is due after expenses; a practical application.

selected.text: Therefore they must keep accounts and make claims, as they themselves are in debt and payment of debts is necessary. As He, glorified and exalted be He, has said: "The payment of debts is an urgent obligation."
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter requires keeping accounts and making claims, citing His words that payment of debts is an urgent obligation; a foundational statement on debt.

selected.text: A package was sent addressed to Shabahang. Send it, but in such a way that you can be certain of its arrival. Write the name on the envelope either in his name or that of another person whose receipt is assured
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that a package be sent so its arrival is certain; care in delivery.

selected.text: some difficulties had arisen in Samandar's business affairs, and the friends in Qazvin decided there should be a separation between the two parties … that pure heart to remain in anxiety over debts and distress
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes a business separation decided by the friends of Qazvin and the anxiety of debts it left; the human cost of failed partnerships.

selected.text: Take care of that house because the light of the love of God was ignited in it. The Fragrances of the Kingdom of Abha perfumed the nostrils. As thou art obliged, there is no harm done if thou desires to rent it.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a house where the love of God was kindled be cared for while permitting rental; care for a meaningful place.

selected.text: Instruct the sons of Jinab-i-Adib and Jinab-i-Ibn-i-Abhar and give them funds to build the graves of those two noble ones. If they are unable, select one of the friends to quickly build those two honored graves
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs funds for building the graves of two noble believers; care for memorials.

selected.text: Regarding the purchase of two houses adjacent to the Shrine that you had written about, I wrote to Aqa Siyyid Mahdi that first Aqa Siyyid Isma'il must fully pay off his debts, and then attend to this important task.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that debts be paid before buying houses adjacent to the Shrine; debts before acquisitions.

selected.text: You had written that the German government wants to send your dear husband for service either to Iran or to Africa … he must make firm arrangements beforehand - that is, regarding salary he must make a firm contract
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises that a husband sent abroad by his government make a firm contract regarding salary beforehand; the guide’s example of a clear agreement.

selected.text: And as for the gaz - We have sent it to thee; use it as thou pleasest, though the Wronged One preferreth it pure, without almonds
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh sends gaz, noting His preference for it pure without almonds; an intimate detail of daily life.

selected.text: Half of the funds remain outstanding; therefore, We did not wish to issue a decree in this regard. Half of the funds have reached them; We await the remainder, after which whatever is commanded will be most acceptable.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh withholds a decree while half the funds remain outstanding; patience until obligations are complete.

selected.text: Regarding the receipts you had written about - we presented that amount to you. Praise be to God there is no burden. The wealth belongs to God and we have presented it to one who is attracted by the fragrances of God.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá releases a believer from a sum noted in receipts, saying the wealth belongs to God and was presented to one attracted by His fragrances; generosity in accounts.

selected.text: The sister and mother of his honor Aqa Siyyid Mahdi have ascended to the eternal realm. They had some water rights in Nayriz which they left to this servant. I accepted it and bestowed it upon his honor Aqa Siyyid Mahdi
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá accepts water rights bequeathed to him by two departed women and bestows them on their relative Áqá Siyyid Mahdí; a gift received and passed on within the family.

selected.text: And it was written that from a certain place an amount of thirty tumans would be sent for their expenses. If it has not arrived, Jinab-i-Samandar or others should give it and later when it arrives they can receive it back
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter directs that friends advance expenses if a promised sum has not arrived, to be repaid later; practical bridging of delays.

selected.text: regarding the forty-seven pounds that was transferred but did not reach you. This caused extreme embarrassment and shame. I know not in what language to apologize. In any case, this matter was written about to Jinab-i-Amin.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá apologizes deeply that a transfer of forty-seven pounds did not arrive; accountability for undelivered payments.

selected.text: Jinab-i-Luhrasb Khan must first pay his debts, and whatever property remains after that, the rights should be determined and delivered to Jinab-i-Amin … use the proceeds from two-sixths of the farm according to the endowment
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that debts be paid first before remaining property is divided according to rights and endowment; priority of creditors.

selected.text: In the world of humanity there are few institutions as fruitful as the Gulistan Company. This zealous company strives to rescue the ascended souls and purified bodies from the clutches of crows and ravens and predatory birds.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises the Gulistan Company, which rescues the bodies of the departed from predatory birds, as among the most fruitful institutions; a distinctive enterprise of service.

selected.text: Regarding the electrical trade, strive in every way to gain complete mastery, so that when I need you with the electrical machine and electric light in the Holy Land, you will be able to operate the electrical machine and illuminate the electric lights and charge the electric carriage with power and set it in motion.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges an electrician to gain complete mastery of his trade so that he may later serve in the Holy Land; a vivid call to excellence of skill.

selected.text: As to what thou hast mentioned regarding business and transactions, these matters have been made dependent in the Book of God upon consultation. Let them consult with faithful and upright souls concerning their business dealings and the like, and whatsoever is decided, let them act upon it, placing their trust in God.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh states that business dealings depend in the Book of God upon consultation with faithful and upright souls, followed by action with trust in God; the guide’s foundational text on consultation in commerce.

selected.text: Now that circumstances have brought about difficulties in their affairs, it is incumbent and obligatory upon us to assist them to the extent possible, nay beyond what is possible. Therefore, if feasible, arrange without delay five hundred tumans and deliver it to Aqa Mirza Abdullah, descendant of His Holiness Samandar.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls assisting a family in difficulty obligatory, “nay beyond what is possible,” and sends five hundred tumans; a strong statement of duty to help.

selected.text: The most difficult issue is your debts in Yazd. These debts must be given thought. In all matters correspond and consult with the honored branch Aqa Mirza Mahmud. His affairs are also in disarray. Make some arrangement, for until affairs are organized, liberation from debts is difficult, and debt is a great affliction.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls debt a great affliction and urges consultation and order in affairs as the path to liberation from it; combines obligation with consultation.

selected.text: From the circumstances, it appears that no prosperity has been achieved there, but you had not written whether there is hope for prosperity in the future or not … according to what has been heard, he has become employed in minor work with one of the divine friends who gives him one hundred and twenty ghurush per month
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes that no prosperity has been achieved in a place and that a man has found modest employment; a realistic view of uncertain livelihoods.

selected.text: Tell Bahman ibn Jamshid that hereafter every span of the remaining land will fetch an exorbitant price, and that is better for them than an extensive burial ground. Nevertheless, if His Honor the Afnan of the Blessed Tree considers it advisable to exchange this land with their own burial ground, that too is permissible.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes that remaining land will fetch a high price, better than an extensive burial ground, yet permits an exchange if the Afnán advises it; judgment between value and need.

selected.text: For the time being, His Holiness Afnan Aqa Siyyid Husayn, upon him be the Glory of God, and you must quickly collect his outstanding claims in that region and deliver them to his survivors. You must certainly make the utmost effort until the final portion is quickly received, receipts obtained, and sent to the Holy Land.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges quick collection of a deceased man’s claims for his survivors, with receipts; care for heirs through diligent collection.

selected.text: Concerning what was mentioned about the matter of trade, it was presented, and He said: "Act according to what the honored Afnan, Siyyid M. - upon him be My glory and loving-kindness - deemeth advisable. His wealth is God's wealth. This is a firm, verified, and established command, to which honored servants bear witness."
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh directs that trade follow the advice of the Afnán, Siyyid M., whose wealth He calls God’s wealth; an instance of deferring to a trusted counselor.

selected.text: God hath forbidden you to sell to any save your own people, nor to purchase from others, that ye may, in your religion, conduct commerce amongst yourselves according to what God hath permitted you therein. Say: Verily the earth, and the water, and the air, and the fire are yours, if ye be of them that testify to the truth.
selected.reason: The Báb’s Book of Names forbids selling to or buying from any but one’s own people; a provision in its distinct revelatory setting.

selected.text: And regarding the matter of the name H, do whatever you deem advisable. As he wrote, it is difficult, for here no one is seen who intends to send funds to the land of A and land of M. In any case, do whatever you deem advisable. If you intend to engage in trade and seek profit, in this case request it - there is no objection.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter leaves a difficult matter to the addressee’s judgment and raises no objection if he intends to engage in trade and seek profit; freedom of choice in commerce.

selected.text: There were some times when this servant was immersed in a sea of debts. The people of weakness had opened doors of expenditure that were beyond endurance. Despite this, with utmost patience it was managed through loans and assets until they themselves declared their independence. Then the debts were settled through separation.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls being immersed in a sea of debts from others’ expenditure and settling them patiently; a personal narrative of managing debt.

selected.text: As for the amount of profit in cash transactions, the Bab (may my spirit be sacrificed for Him) permitted commercial profit, but the Blessed Beauty commanded reduction as much as possible. And if dispute and conflict arise, its judgment is referred to the House of Justice. And as for impermissible profit, it is excessive profit.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that the Báb permitted commercial profit while Bahá’u’lláh commanded its reduction, referring disputes to the House of Justice; distinct settings of a law.

selected.text: As for the properties of the honorable Nawwab, upon him be 966 [Baha'u'llah], he and a group of acquaintances are exerting their utmost efforts, as they have done before, and God willing they shall triumph and prevail according to the meaning of "the party of God shall be victorious." That is, they shall obtain and deliver your rights
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter reports the efforts of the honorable Nawwáb and his acquaintances to recover properties and deliver the addressee’s rights; persistence in securing rights.

selected.text: Regarding what you wrote about the remainder of the estate of Muhammad, upon him be the Glory of God, if it were to be deposited in the House of God in the name of those two children, it would be closer to righteousness, for it may be that their mother might not spend it on the children, as she has set her heart upon another husband.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter advises depositing an estate in the children’s name lest their mother not spend it on them; protecting children’s inheritance.

selected.text: May they not dissolve this company partnership. I hope that through divine favors this partnership will be blessed, for all the pillars of this partnership are firm and steadfast and are known for their divine love in that region. Therefore it is not appropriate that this partnership be dissolved and this sign of blessing be abrogated.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a firm and loving partnership not be dissolved; shows the value placed on stable cooperation.

selected.text: Praise be to God that he, in obedience to God's command, wrote his will in his own hand before his ascension and left everyone at ease and comfort. Obedience to divine commands is the cause of the comfort of creation. Just observe this one matter - how much the will has become the cause of tranquility of hearts and ease of soul and mind.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá praises a believer who wrote his will before his passing, leaving everyone at ease; the will as a cause of tranquility.

selected.text: Regarding the purchase of the shrine and tomb of His Holiness Manshadi, complete and thorough instructions were given to Jinab-i-Aqa Ahmad. However, he said that he would undertake the purchase of the land after his journey, as he is now planning to travel to Europe. If he were to take action now, it would not be done in a fitting manner.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains a deferred shrine purchase so that it may be done fittingly; timing in property acquisition.

selected.text: I am thinking of her land (here). Let her make Mirza Hadi her representative, that is, she should send Mirza Hadi a written authorization signed by the Government (American) so that Mirza Hadi may, in her behalf, turn the land in her name. The Government, however, should clearly state that Mirza Hadi is authorized to buy the land for her.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises a written, government-certified authorization for a representative to buy land; representation done properly.

selected.text: As for expenses, what was submitted was not easy, despite the necessity. In other instances that amount was submitted for this purpose, therefore expenses should be moderated as much as possible. Now 50 pounds have been arranged somehow - it couldn't be sent by telegram so was sent by post. If expenses are this high, the means are not available
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that expenses be moderated as means are limited; prudence in spending.

selected.text: Concerning the situation in Alexandria which thou hadst written about, and the abundance of debts and the depreciation of currency - this is truly a difficult matter. I hope that through the grace and favor of the Blessed Beauty this difficulty too will be resolved, affairs will again be set in order, and comfort and ease will be attained by all.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá acknowledges debts and currency depreciation in Alexandria and hopes for restored order and ease for all; compassion amid economic distress.

selected.text: Referring to the goldsmith's shop that belongs to the Cause of God and has been entrusted to his custody: Since one-third of the shares of the non-existent inheritors reverts to the House of Justice when it is formed, and in its absence the Centre of the Covenant, therefore please pay the amount due to the share of the rent to Haji Hasan's daughter.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs rent shares for a goldsmith’s shop and the heirs’ portion; inheritance and rent.

selected.text: Concerning His Honour the Physician, upon him be the Glory of God and His favours, they wrote that according to instructions it was written to him to provide details about the House - how much had been received, how much remained, and likewise what were the costs of repairs. In any case, matters should now proceed with utmost brevity until news arrives.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter asks for details of how much was received and remains for the House and what repairs cost; accountability for building funds.

selected.text: That is, it must be sent to Dr. Muhammad Khan Mahallati in Paris, because he had previously supervised Ibtihaj's sons and for this service had received an annual stipend from the honored Ibtihaj. However, since I sent the sons to Beirut, this salary arrangement is terminated, but as means of uplifting his spirit, send him this money because he is in need.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá sends money to a man whose stipend ended because he is in need; assistance beyond contractual obligation.

selected.text: The custodianship of the Blessed House has been granted to the exalted leaf, the wife of the Primal Point, and her sister, upon both be My Glory of God, My Bounty and My Favor. … Before God, we have conferred this custodianship on the House and thus have We adorned it with Our Benevolence, and arrayed Our command with the evidence of His Might and Compassion
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh grants the custodianship of the Blessed House to the wife of the Báb and her sister; a distinctive act of custodianship.

selected.text: Regarding the water rights given to Aqa Siyyid Mahdi - their return is not permitted unless his brothers indicate that this inheritance belongs to all and should be divided … Regarding the two hundred tumans belonging to the daughter of Haji 'Ammih Khanum - we have accepted that and gifted it to her herself … Send fifty tumans for Aqa Siyyid Zaynu'l-'Abidin
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá rules on water rights, returns a gift to a daughter and sends a sum to another; careful dealings with inheritance and gifts.

selected.text: As to what was written concerning the House, after submission they stated that whatever belongs to you should revert to the Truth. At present in that land there is no one who can attend to affairs and act as is befitting. Therefore if someone is found who can repair it and dwell therein, this would be acceptable; otherwise, it would be preferable to sell it.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh directs that a house be repaired and lived in, or else sold; practical stewardship.

selected.text: Sometimes caravans come from Beirut to this land. Since the land route lacks security, therefore your honor should observe - if a reliable caravan is departing, travel in its company, otherwise wait and depart by sea vessel. Utmost care in this matter is certainly necessary, as it is absolutely not permitted to travel without a reliable caravan by this route.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter advises travel only with a reliable caravan; prudence in risk.

selected.text: Since I had previously endowed the crystal shop next to the mosque and the property of Zaman-Abad and others, and according to the law of the Kitab-i-Aqdas all endowments revert to the Huquq, therefore you must be content with this. I submitted that these endowments would revert later, and now something must be done that will serve the needs of the Cause today.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter notes that endowments revert to the Ḥuqúq according to the Kitáb-i-Aqdas; law on endowments.

selected.text: And regarding the House matter, certainly give it utmost importance and be very careful that the court does not betray. Convey my greetings to the Consulate's translator and say that I ask this of you - that judgment be rendered with justice. Certainly you will exert your utmost effort and I will never forget your service as long as I live and it will be rewarded.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that a court be watched so the House matter is judged with justice; defending property rights.

selected.text: With gold in hand, often I was refused provision. They would tell me roughly:- we do not have straw nor barley. I would answer: "Are we not your guests passing through your country and has not the prophet said 'be ye kind to your guest if he were infidel.'" They would then frown and say: "we will not sell you anything." I answer: "All right. Give to me then gratis."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts being refused provisions despite having gold and appealing to hospitality; pressure in trade.

selected.text: to his honor Afnan, upon him be my glory and my loving-kindness: You made no mention of the affairs of Beirut and Constantinople, and from the beginning no permission was sought nor consultation undertaken, despite all being commanded to this. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter rebukes lack of consultation yet delivers the House’s funds; accountability with forbearance.

selected.text: Concerning what you wrote about the funds that Jinab-i-Ism-i-N and Jinab-i-Ism-i-'Ayn, upon them be the Glory of God, have sent, and that you have used some for your debts and bestowed some upon others - this servant submitted this before His presence. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh approves the use of sent funds for debts and gifts, permission having been given beforehand; trust in a steward.

selected.text: Now, since the affairs of Mirza Abdul-Hussein, upon him be the Glory of God, the Most Glorious, are in disarray, you must assist him in every way possible so that, God willing, he may fully pay off these debts, for addressing this situation in such a way that leaves no cause for complaint or objection from the creditors will preserve the reputation of the loved ones of God.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges helping a believer pay his debts so creditors have no complaint and the friends’ reputation is preserved; mutual help with integrity.

selected.text: And concerning what was written about His Honor the Effendi - may God, blessed and exalted be He, strengthen him - having willed to send quince from that direction to this direction: yes, quince is good and is also available in this city. And if distinguished trees from there can be sent without trouble, and likewise the Mastaki apricots that were mentioned, it would be beloved
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter welcomes quince, trees and apricots if sent without trouble; care in provisions.

selected.text: As for the matter of the Prince's wife, I have not heard such news until now and there are no such events occurring within. However, regarding the journey to Yazd for the purpose of arranging and preparing to pay debts - this is very appropriate. You must strive night and day to pay the debts and be freed from these entanglements. In truth, you are in great difficulty and hardship.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá approves a journey to arrange payment of debts and urges striving night and day to be freed from them, acknowledging the debtor’s hardship; obligation with sympathy.

selected.text: News of the organization of the affairs of the storehouse, the attainment of confirmation from the Lord of Bounties, and the payment and settlement of the claims of eighty-four persons has brought continuous joy. Through the grace and bounty of that Beloved One Who cherishes His servants, I hope that complete liberation will be achieved and that this will bring peace of mind to you.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá rejoices at the settlement of the claims of eighty-four persons on a storehouse; a positive outcome of financial restoration.

selected.text: If today the dwelling of the Most Pure Consort - upon Her be all glory and exaltation - in the true house would cause clamor among the servants and become the cause of rancor and hatred, residence therein is not permitted, according to the wisdom which God hath revealed in the Book, until God bringeth about His appointed time. In any case, observance of wisdom is necessary and obligatory, and if in these days, due to wisdom and expediency, the residence of the Consort and Afnan in that house is not feasible, its door must remain closed and no one is permitted to dwell
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh forbids residence in a house if it would cause rancor, leaving its door closed; wisdom over property use.

selected.text: It was that venerable personage, Bahjet Jurjus Jamal, a man of crystalline intellect and pure heart, albeit one of fervent Protestant conviction, from whom I sought to purchase the land where the pine trees stood. He did, however, with steadfast resolution decline the transaction, quoting the formidable sum of ten thousand pounds. This hallowed spot he had planted with his own hands and had solemnly enjoined upon his brother that not even a cubit or span of that consecrated ground should be sold to any soul.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts a landowner refusing to sell land he had planted; respect for others’ attachment to property.

selected.text: his honor Afnan - upon him be the Most Glorious Glory - hath written that they have acquired a piece of land in that region dedicated to the name of God, exalted be His glory. After being presented at the Most Holy Court, it was honored with acceptance, and They commanded: "Write to 'Ali-Qabl-i-Akbar, upon him be My glory, that the construction and development of that place rests with you
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh accepts land dedicated to God and entrusts its development to a believer; dedicated property and responsibility.

selected.text: The house that belongs to the Afnan of the Blessed Tree, His Holiness Haji Siyyid Mihdi, upon him be the Glory of God the Most Glorious, should be renovated by himself - there should be no partner or participant in that renovation. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá directs that an owner renovate his house himself without partners; respect for ownership.

selected.text: In reference to the large house which thou hadst explained, thou shouldst take into consideration Mr. Jeffery Parsons' consent, pleasure and joy. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises renting the larger house with the co-owner’s consent and placing farms in suitable care; consent and economy in managing property.

selected.text: Now that they will not sell the Bukhara properties, strive to have the heirs quickly agree to sell the 'Ishqabad properties and pay the debt. Write continuously to the heirs and awaken them, otherwise it will become like the story of Jinab-i-Haji Mirza Hasan. Since this is the case, the six hundred and seventy pounds you have given is enough, for the purpose was to clear the debt of the Afnan.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges heirs to sell properties promptly and pay the debt of the Afnán; responsibility of heirs for debts.

selected.text: This matter was discussed with Aqa 'Abdu's-Samad, upon him be God's peace. He mentioned that he thought they were not in debt, but later it became known they owed considerable sums. If Haji Muhammad's funds do not arrive, that land will lose all credibility with foreigners, just as this land has.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter reports a refusal to advance funds because “it is not my money but the people’s money”; distinguishes personal generosity from the duty of one holding others’ funds.

selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter directs that heirs acting under a will send funds to a named trustee; execution of a will through a trustee.

selected.text: you know that 'Abdu'l-Baha does not accept a single penny without necessity, for hoarding is never befitting. The travel expenses, praise be to God, are ready and prepared. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns an unneeded gift, saying he accepts nothing without necessity, since hoarding is unbefitting; the guide’s instance of gifts accepted only under need.

selected.text: According to His command, wisdom must be observed in all cases, especially regarding the Afnan, upon them be all the most glorious Glory. This has been repeatedly emphasized. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter stresses that wisdom must be observed in all cases and the Afnán protected in all conditions; care for a family amid financial affairs.

selected.text: Regarding what was written about the funds for the Most Exalted Leaf, upon her be the Most Glorious of all Glory - what was sent has been received, however the remainder should reach the Supreme [Lady] the Leaf, her mother. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter directs funds for the Most Exalted Leaf and leaves the choice of garments to her mother; care for a family’s dignity.

selected.text: Since there was no deed of ownership in hand, and the deed was in the name of one of the friends who had passed away, the oppressors first claimed that the owner of the house - meaning that purchaser - died without heirs, therefore this house belongs to the government. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts a house appropriated by oppressors because the deed was in a deceased friend’s name; the importance of secure title.

selected.text: Praise be to God, you succeeded in having several financial officers appointed from America for Iran, and God willing you will also succeed in securing a loan for Iran from America. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá contrasts hoped-for American loans to Iran with European loans that, through self-interested intermediaries, yielded only loss; a national-scale lesson on honest finance.

selected.text: His honor Mirza Habibu'llah … had an appointment in Egypt with Muqtadir'ul-Mulk at a salary of five hundred tumans. When Muqtadir'ul-Mulk traveled to Europe, he told him to return from Egypt. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes a man left destitute when his post ended and urges every effort to secure him an appointment; a vivid case of seeking employment for another.

selected.text: You had complained about financial hardship and excessive debts and oppressive creditors … Today a Christian person unhesitatingly demanded repayment of a debt and showed no consideration for our acquaintance, as money is his desired goal and consideration is completely lacking. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá shares his own experience of a creditor who showed no consideration and the extension he obtained with difficulty; a personal account of debt pressure.

selected.text: upon him be the Glory of God, during his presence, having resided in this land for some time, became aware of the confined space. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter recounts the search for land in Akka and an owner demanding an exorbitant price; context for the reported purchase.

selected.text: This house which they are now selling must certainly be purchased soon, as it is very important. Surely you and the divine friends will make the utmost effort in this important matter. However, we will manage to provide one thousand tumans by whatever means possible.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges the purchase of an important house and pledges a thousand tumans despite limited means; priority given to a significant property.

selected.text: As to their turning towards this direction, it is not permitted, for conditions are unsettled, as was explained before. selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh permits use but not sale of properties needed by a lady; preserving means of support.

selected.text: Praise be to God, means of trade and blessing have again been obtained for you. … As for Mirza Isma'il Mishkat, praise be to God that lamp was kindled in the glass of pardon and forgiveness and became illumined in the hidden world's niche. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá rejoices at renewed means of trade and asks that a deceased believer’s hard-to-sell effects go to the poor and his grave be built fittingly; joins commerce with care for the departed.

selected.text: If a friend dies and leaves behind some debt, the believers must do their utmost to pay it off to the very last cent. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reported words direct the believers to pay a deceased friend’s debts to the last cent and recall his own scrupulous payment of such debts; a strong communal obligation.

selected.text: Zakat on gold, after it reaches twenty dinars, shall be half a dinar when it is minted and a year consisting of eleven months according to the Book of God hath passed over it. When it exceeds that amount by four dinars, three-fifths of a dinar is due on it, and thus God hath ordained up to its prescribed limit. If thou desirest to remove from thyself the ordinance of Zakat, then keep the gold in ingots, though I do not like this for anyone. God hath ordained the Zakat on silver similar to gold in terms of the passing of a year and its being minted, after it reaches two hundred dirhams. At that point, five dirhams are obligatory upon its owner by God's decree
selected.reason: The Báb’s Epistle of Justice sets the zakát on gold and silver; a law in its own setting.

selected.text: Then it was reported that each one had designated or would designate a sum, and that merchandise would be sent to him from wherever he requested … Repeatedly some complained that Aqa Muhammad-'Ali was not sending merchandise according to requests - that he was sending items contrary to what was ordered … your letter arrived mentioning a theft, saying "They broke my safe and took three hundred and fifty liras
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter recounts merchandise disputes and a theft from a safe; a narrative of conflict in commercial arrangements.

selected.text: Concerning the matter of partnership about which they wrote, permission was first granted as previously explained, and now it has been referred to the honored Ism'u'llah [Name of God]. He will write you the details. All the gentlemen -- may the Most Glorious Glory of God be upon them -- have the utmost love for you. Their purpose in mentioning these matters is to protect wealth from the thieves and traitors of the world.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter explains that counsel on a partnership aimed to protect wealth from the thieves and traitors of the world; a reason behind caution in partnerships.

selected.text: For the repair of the honored House in Baghdad we collected one thousand two hundred and fifty tumans and deposited it with Haji 'Abdu'r-Rasul in 'Ishqabad until gradually a sufficient amount could be collected … The late Aqa Mirza 'Ali-Naqi had made a bequest, and since its execution was not possible at that time, a share of his timchih was designated, and Jinab-i-Aqa Siyyid Nasru'llah has sent all the rent from that share
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts funds collected for repairing the House in Baghdad and a bequest’s rent; the guide’s example of funds and circumstances.

selected.text: Regarding the inquiry about Huquq, how much should be paid on nineteen mithqals - God's ordinance has been set at nineteen percent. It was also asked whether, if it exceeds nineteen, it must reach another nineteen or if the excess is also subject to Huquq. Whatever exceeds nineteen is not subject to Huquq until it reaches another nineteen. … As commanded, write to Nun and Jim that wherever divine Huquq remains unpaid, they should collect it and send it to Jinab-i-Amin or Jinab-i-Samandar, upon them be the Glory of God, obtain a receipt, and report back so that action may be taken according to His will

selected.text: During the time that His Holiness the Exalted One lived in Bushihr and was in the trading business, a few merchants bought some Prussian blue dye from His blessed Person. When their negotiations were over, the goods were delivered to their office and the time came to settle the account. But they abandoned their agreement and began bargaining anew. This was the practice of the merchants in Bushihr in former days. When the transaction was concluded, the buyer would dismiss the contract and begin renegotiating, in order to get a better price or a discount. Consequently, the merchants reneged on the price. However, His Holiness did not agree to it. They persisted, but He responded, "Our negotiations were completed. If you do not want to buy [the goods], cancel the contract altogether
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts the Báb in Bushihr refusing merchants who reneged on a settled price; a memorable example of firm integrity in trade.

selected.text: At last I went to an Arab friend of mine and borrowed from him £2[0] at 2 per cent. This money I took to a merchant who was in former time a grain-dealer but now out of work. I told him We will enter into a partnership, the Capital from me, the labor from you. With this fund you will deal four months in grain. After paying off all the expenses of rent etc; and receiving your monthly salary, we will divide the net profit; one third for you and two third for me. We entered into this agreement and he engaged in business. After four months we cleared our accounts. I payed the debt with its two per cent; the merchant received his one third of the net profit, all the other expenses defrayed and 80 pounds left in the balance for me. With that sum, then I built a bath in the house which is kept intact up to the present day
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts a grain partnership with capital and labor shared, debts repaid and profit divided; a distinctive narrative of fair partnership.

selected.text: As for the land in Port Said, when the late respected father was in Port Said and was planning to return to Shiraz, he wrote to me asking that I instruct Aqa Ahmad to purchase Mirza Aqa's land, as funds were needed for the journey. I wrote to Aqa Ahmad at that time, and Aqa Ahmad purchased that land and sent me the official documents and papers, which are among my papers. After the departure of the Afnan, Aqa Ahmad requested these documents. I wrote that I did not have time to locate these papers which were stored away with books and Tablets. Therefore, I asked him to write again to the Afnan to obtain and send a deed from Aqa Mirza Aqa, which the Afnan obtained and sent at that time. This transaction was conducted through me, and those original documents are preserved among my papers, though time is needed to search for and send them.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recounts a Port Said land transaction and preserved documents; financial memory and documentation.

selected.text: When Aqa Mirza 'Abdu'l-Husayn was departing, I wished to present him with travel expenses, but due to scarcity of funds it was not possible. It was arranged that he would borrow from his fellow traveler and you would repay it there. Please deliver one hundred tumans, and henceforth if you send [...], stipulate that the German consul here should deliver gold, not bank notes, as they depreciate greatly and people accept them only reluctantly with a discount. Thus far through the United Company, one sum of two hundred pounds has arrived, another of two hundred and fifty, and a third of two hundred and ten, and another telegram has come from the United Company saying they have sent two hundred and fifty, but it has not yet arrived. selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá details borrowed travel funds, gold over depreciating notes, and debts with interest; financial detail of travel.

selected.text: As to what was written concerning the House and his honor Mirza regarding [Baha'u'llah]: their best course is to say what they had said at first and acknowledge that all these properties belong there. If from the beginning, during the upheavals in that land, they had spoken truthfully and stated that these properties were not theirs, none of these matters would have occurred and they would have found themselves at ease in every way. For His Holiness and they themselves know that in this place nothing even as fine as a hair has emerged or will emerge that deviates from justice and fairness, and their interests would certainly have been protected in any case. A hundred thousand regrets that one should be heedless of what benefits them and be unaware of their own harm and benefit. All their properties revert to this place according to valid deeds, but when the decree of imprisonment, trials and emigration came to pass, they did not release even one house.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter regrets that truthful acknowledgment of property ownership would have prevented troubles; honesty in property.

selected.text: from the annual income man must deduct his yearly expenditure. Then from residue 19 percent must be given as Huquq. This means that during the year a personal income from his business is 1000 pounds. His yearly expenditure, which amounts to 600 pounds, must be deducted. Four hundred pounds will be the residue. From this 400 pounds nineteen percent Huquq must be taken. That is, from every hundred pounds of this 400 pounds, nineteen percent, whose total will be 76 pounds, which must be taken as Huquq, to be spent for benevolent purposes (public interests). … From all property every year Huquq should not be taken. A person may possess 100,000 pounds. It is not possible for him to give Huquq from this 100,000 pounds every year. For instance thou shouldst deliver thy yearly expenditure from what thy income in one year is, and then from the residue thou should pay Huquq. But the property (income) for last year whose Huquq hath already been paid, this year hath no more Huquq to be paid
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that Ḥuqúq is paid on income after expenses and not repeatedly on the same property; a clear worked explanation.

selected.text: Another matter concerns the return of the beloved of the heart, His Honour Amin, upon him be God's peace and favors. Until now, which is nearly a year, nothing substantial has arrived. That beloved one is aware that in these days they wrote to this servant that if you wish to receive two hundred Ottoman liras from the beloved His Honour Shaykh, upon him be Baha'u'llah's glory, the funds are available here. They wished to send it to His Honour, the beloved of the heart, upon him be the Most Glorious Beauty of Baha'u'llah, and they also sent some to purchase and send silk from Rasht. Then they suspended it, writing that they feared it might result in loss like the shawl of the previous year. In any case, if possible, they should send it. That beloved one is aware of the affairs here and the expenses of this land
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter recounts suspended funds for fear of loss and the expenses of the Holy Land; timing and caution in transfers.

selected.text: Among the foundations of the prosperity and development of countries, human comfort, orderly conditions, and worldly happiness of nations and peoples is the establishment of companies, for major enterprises cannot be undertaken except through companies. This is the very thing that is the cause of the complete success and prosperity of the Western nations today. From the all-encompassing confirmation of the Ancient Beauty, it is known and certain that companies will soon be formed in Iran and great benefits and advantages will result. However, at present the friends in Iran are afflicted with famine and high prices and are in complete hardship. Such companies are formed from surplus capital beyond what is needed. If announced now, it will not succeed and will cause humiliation to the Cause of God, just as a company was announced in Egypt, and since it did not ultimately materialize, it caused distress of mind and became the cause of general sorrow and great coldness, resulting in complete embarrassment before outsiders.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls companies a foundation of national prosperity yet advises delay amid famine, since companies are formed from surplus capital and a failed announcement harms the Cause; the guide’s key qualification of resources and preparedness.

selected.text: Be thou a trafficker of the spirit and with the choicest merchandise acceptable in the presence of the All-Merciful travel from this contingent world to the Placeless Country of the Well-Beloved. In this wise shall thine every apparent loss be transformed into limitless gain and every damage bring forth profit in the Garden of His divine good pleasure. … For at the end of the day profit in this evanescent realm is naught but loss and gain brings only ruination. When thou dost enter the market place of the All-Merciful which is in the divine Kingdom, however, thou shalt become the manifestation of His grace and bountiful favour. … There wilt thou find the merchandise that real kings might long for and thus wilt thou become a judge of true gems. In thy palm shalt thou hold pearls unparalleled and rubies and corals too. Herein lies real business and true commerce. … Seek for this kind of magnificent profit and strive to obtain this glorious treasure as much as is within thy power so that thou shalt amass exceeding wealth and abundant riches
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the believer a trafficker of the spirit whose every loss becomes gain in the marketplace of the All-Merciful; the guide’s fullest statement of spiritual commerce.

selected.text: This evanescent servant has been seized with bewilderment at the events that have transpired, swimming in an ocean of perplexity and contemplation, for what has occurred in the Great City has harmed the trustworthiness, religiosity, truthfulness and sincerity of the believers. The rest is clear to that beloved one - what has passed and what is now passing. Aqa Muhammad 'Ali's (of the Land of Sad) occupation was separate, his affairs distinct, having no connection whatsoever with the Shaykh - upon him be 9 66 [Baha'u'llah]. Nevertheless, he tore away the veil of contentment and arose with complete greed to harm and show enmity toward the Shaykh. Would that he had sufficed with himself alone! Day and night, before those within and without, he was aflame with the fire of greed and strove diligently to destroy the Shaykh's work. And according to what is known, the Shaykh's trade was also confused for two reasons: for whatever one would build up, another would tear down, and in some transactions losses
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s letter laments greed that harmed trustworthiness and the Shaykh’s trade; consequences of rivalry.
